title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1LC1LB_1RD1LD_1RE0RA_---0LB_0LF0RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1LC1LB_1RD1LD_1RE0RA_---0LB_0LF0RC.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and probably out of reach. The tape is two growing blocks followed by a short list of counters. The first counter loses 1 every few epochs; when it runs out, the machine either halts (the halting configurations are proved in Lean) or turns one of its blocks into a new, much larger counter. Which of the two happens is decided by remainders of numbers produced by a Collatz-like map. The first run-out, at step 2.995·1023, did not halt; the second is due after about 10^(1011) steps, far beyond exact simulation.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 55,171 cells have been visited and 35,148 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.462). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: The two growth phases
claims.text: Y n p R = 0^inf D> 0111011 (011)^n (1011)^p R: Y n p (1111 R) reaches Y (n+1) (p+1) R in 10n+10p+35 steps, and Y n p ((1110)^(k+2) 1 R) reaches Y (n+2) (p+1) ((1110)^(k+1) 1 R) in 20n+20p+86 steps, for all n, p, k and every tape R; both iterated.

claims.title: A marker in front of the last counter halts
claims.text: For all n, p, k the configurations with run lists 3 2^n 3^p 5 3^k 1 and 3 2^n 3^(p+1) 1 3^k 1 halt: the marker walks through the last counter, one run per two visits, and the machine stops at the right end of the tape (E reads a 0 past the last run).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>210</sup> steps
claims.text: An exact macro simulation (blocks of 12 cells with one block of context) with linear cycle jumps from bbtools.cycles runs to 10210 steps without a halt. accel.py check compares it with the plain macro run.

claims.title: The first counter ran out at step 2.995·10<sup>23</sup>, without a halt
claims.text: The counter that starts at 22 (step 6,183) reaches 0 at step 2.995·1023. No marker is in front at that moment: the block of 103,352,228,706 runs of 3 becomes a new counter, the old last counter (4) is absorbed, and the tail becomes 3^131245843096 s 3^103352228710 1. The new first counter has lost 143 by 10159 steps and 199 by 10210 (about one per factor of ten in steps), so it runs out after about 10^(1011) steps.
claims.where: py/runlist.py events 27 (events 55 to 59); inside the range where the run-list simulator agrees with the accelerated macro run

claims.title: The run-list rules
claims.text: At the left-end visits in state D the tape is 3 2^n 3^p FRONT 3^X s 3^k1 s 3^k2 1 (run lengths; separators s = 0, 2, 4). Three local rules (proved in Lean) and a table of eleven events at the separators (learned from the plain machine by affine fits on small instances and checked on far ones) give a simulator that agrees with the plain machine at every visit to 3·109 steps and with the accelerated macro run, tape and step count, at all 3,172 visits up to 3.4·10158 steps. To leading order the number of pairs K at the start of an epoch follows K' = 3K/4 + X or 3K/4.

claims.title: A run-out can halt, and does in a minority of cases
claims.text: Started from the configuration of step 1.1·10<sup>27</sup> with the first counter replaced by J, the run-list simulator halts for J = 0, 3, 6 and goes on (with two or three new counters of 15 to 28 digits) for J = 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 to 29. With the number of pairs varied as well (J = 2, 5, 9, twenty values each) 7 of 60 runs halt. So the structure does not exclude a halt: it is one outcome of a run-out, chosen by remainders. If each run-out halted independently with a probability bounded away from 0, the machine would halt eventually, but the next run-out is about 10^(10<sup>11</sup>) steps away.

claims.title: No halt in the first 6.44×10<sup>2890</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 6.44×102890 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 2.56×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 10,834 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. A proof of non-halting would have to show that no run-out ever lets a marker through; a proof of halting needs the remainders of 10<sup>11</sup>-digit numbers produced by a Collatz-like map with no known shortcut.

check: python3 runlist.py check 3e9        # run lists against the plain machine, every visit
python3 accel.py check 1e12         # accelerated macro run against the plain macro run
python3 runlist.py events 27        # the events to 10^27 steps; the run-out is events 55 to 59
python3 runlist.py exhaust 0 30     # what a run-out does for 30 values of the first counter
python3 runlist.py halt "0 3 2^9 3^21 1 3^9 1"   # a marker in front of the last counter: halts

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and this machine is a good candidate for never being decided. Started on a blank tape it has not stopped in 10<sup>210</sup> steps. It keeps a countdown; each time the countdown reaches zero it either stops for good or starts a far longer countdown, and which of the two happens depends on remainders nobody can predict. The first countdown ended at step 3·10<sup>23</sup> without a stop; the second will end after about 10^(10<sup>11</sup>) steps.

facts.text: No halt in an exact accelerated simulation.
A marker that reaches the last counter walks to the end of the tape and the machine stops: proved in Lean for all sizes.
Step of the first run-out. It did not halt; it built counters of 12 digits.
Rough step count of the next run-out.
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 2.56×10<sup>10</sup> steps).

sections.heading: The tape as a list of run lengths
html: Look at the tape each time the head reaches a new leftmost cell (in state D), and write down only the lengths of its runs of 1s, from left to right. From step 1,096 on the list always has the same layout:
3  2^n  3^p   FRONT   3^X  s 3^k1  s 3^k2  1

<svg viewBox='0 0 600 86' role='img' aria-label='layout of the tape: two growing blocks, a front, counters and the fixed end' style='width:100%;max-width:600px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono)'><rect x='4' y='14' width='120' height='24' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='64' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>2^n</text><rect x='124' y='14' width='110' height='24' fill='var(--accent)'/><text x='179' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--bg)'>3^p</text><rect x='234' y='14' width='70' height='24' fill='none' stroke='var(--head)'/><text x='269' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg2)'>front</text><rect x='304' y='14' width='90' height='24' fill='var(--sunk)' stroke='var(--line-strong)'/><text x='349' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>3^X</text><text x='404' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--head)'>s</text><rect x='414' y='14' width='70' height='24' fill='var(--sunk)' stroke='var(--line-strong)'/><text x='449' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>3^k1</text><text x='494' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--head)'>s</text><rect x='504' y='14' width='60' height='24' fill='var(--sunk)' stroke='var(--line-strong)'/><text x='534' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>3^k2</text><text x='580' y='30' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--fg)'>1</text><text x='119' y='60' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>two growing blocks</text><text x='269' y='60' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>being eaten</text><text x='440' y='60' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>counters, cut by separators s</text><text x='440' y='76' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>k1 is the countdown</text></svg>

Here 2^n means n runs of length 2 and 3^p means p runs of length 3: these are the two growing blocks. Behind them comes whatever they are eating at the moment (the front), and then long stretches of runs of 3 cut into counters by separators (a run of length 0, 2 or 4). For example at step 10,629 the list is 3 2^15 3^14 0 3^22 0 3^4 1.
Between two visits only the front changes, by three small rules (all proved in Lean for blocks of any size):

N        ->  3, N-4     a long run loses 4 cells and the block of 3s gains a run
1, N     ->  N+2        a marker (a single 1) takes the next run: 1 3 -> 5 -> 3 1, it has moved one run right
1, 1, N  ->  3, N
and every visit adds one run of 2 at the left. So a marker walks through a counter at one run per two visits, and the two blocks grow all the time.

sections.heading: A Collatz-like map rebuilds the blocks
html: When the front reaches a separator, the head makes one long excursion and the whole block 2^n is rewritten into about n/2 pairs 3 1, which the blocks then eat again at two pairs per three visits. That is one epoch. If K is the number of pairs at the start of an epoch and X the counter in front, the next epoch starts with
K' = 3K/4 + X     or     K' = 3K/4

pairs, up to rounding. Which case applies, and the rounding, depend on the remainders of n and K (odd or even, and so on). This is the same kind of rule as in the Collatz problem (halve if even, triple and add one if odd): simple to apply, but nobody knows how to predict the remainders many rounds ahead. At a separator one more thing can happen, depending on those remainders: a marker arrives at the counter behind the separator, and that counter loses 1.

sections.heading: What happens when the first counter runs out
html: From step 6,183 the counter k1 starts at 22 and loses 1 every few epochs, while each epoch takes about 4 to 8 times as many steps as the one before: it is at 20 at step 47,656, at 6 at step 5.8·1017, and it reaches 0 at step 2.995·1023.
At a run-out there are two possibilities.

• A marker is there. It passes the empty counter and has only the last counter in front of it. It walks through it to the right end of the tape, and the machine halts there. This is proved in Lean for all sizes (halts_marker5, halts_marker1).
  • No marker is there. Then the block 3^p, which has been growing since the start, is cut off and becomes a new counter, and the countdown starts again from a much larger number.

At step 2.995·1023 the second thing happened: the new countdown starts at 131,245,843,096 (and the last counter is now 103,352,228,710). It loses 1 about once per factor of ten in the step count, so it will run out after roughly 10^(1011) steps: a number of steps with about a hundred billion digits.

Would that run-out halt? Experiments with the same kind of configuration and other counter values show both outcomes: of 30 values of the counter, 3 led to a halt and 27 to new counters; of 60 further variations, 7 halted. If every run-out has some fixed chance of halting, the machine halts eventually, with certainty; but each countdown is unimaginably longer than the one before, and deciding any one of them needs the remainders of numbers that cannot even be written down. That is why the question is open.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.462). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 55,171 cells (44,694 left of the start, 39 right), with a density of 1s of 0.637.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: Two growing blocks rebuilt by a Collatz-like map (K' = 3K/4 or 3K/4 + X) drive a short list of counters; when the first counter runs out the machine halts or builds much larger counters, depending on remainders; the first run-out (step 3.0·10<sup>23</sup>) did not halt, the next is due after about 10^(10<sup>11</sup>) steps; open.
family: nested counters driven by a Collatz-like block map
